[GOOD] Strong structural decomposition: Layer 1 (recovery), Layer 2 (state orchestration), Layer 3 (CLI behavior contract) gives clear responsibility boundaries and avoids a god-object CLI command.

[GOOD] Excellent abstraction discipline: `PortLookup`, `IdentityResolver`, and `SQLProber` isolate platform and IO volatility behind DI seams, improving testability and reducing concrete coupling.

[GOOD] Information hiding is materially improved: ownership predicate is centralized and reused for recovery + stop revalidation, which minimizes drift and aligns with stable-abstractions principles.

[GOOD] The explicit `StateSource` + `RecoveryOutcome` model is a solid anti-ambiguity move; it prevents boolean-smell APIs and keeps legacy `State` semantics intact.

[GOOD] Safety-critical invariants are first-class (never stop unowned, stdout/stderr discipline, best-effort persistence), with tests mapped to behavior contract rows—this is architecturally mature for an operational bug fix.

No P0/P1 architectural blockers remain from this review. Remaining concerns are P2-level design hardening and contract hygiene, acceptable to ship with follow-up discipline.

[STRATEGIST]
[GOOD] The plan is now strongly aligned to purpose: it fixes the actual operator pain (false “not running” + inability to stop/start), and does so symmetrically across `status`/`stop`/`start` and internal `EnsureRunning`, which directly addresses the prior “partial fix” failure mode.

[GOOD] Completeness is notably improved: missing, malformed, unreadable, stale, reused PID, read-only PID-dir, and unowned-listener paths are all explicitly modeled with command-by-command behavior contracts and matching acceptance criteria.

[GOOD] The approach follows sound information-hiding boundaries (Parnas): ownership logic is centralized in `Recoverer.checkOwnership`, state healing is isolated from CLI presentation, and config resolution is separated from lifecycle mechanics.

[SECURITY]
## Security Review: PID-file Recovery Plan (GH#3687)

This plan is exceptionally well-thought-out from a security perspective. The council iteration process has addressed most concerns I would typically raise. My review focuses on residual risks and areas where implementation could still go wrong.

---

[GOOD] The five-signal ownership predicate (exe path, argv token-exact match, data-dir canonicalization, port binding, UID match) is a strong defense-in-depth design against silent process adoption. This directly addresses CWE-283 (Unverified Ownership).

[GOOD] Argument-array `exec.Command` throughout, with integer-typed PID/port values, eliminates command injection vectors (CWE-78). The plan explicitly bans shell interpolation and tests enforce it.

[GOOD] Atomic PID-file writes with `O_NOFOLLOW`, `O_EXCL`, temp+rename, mode 0600, and parent directory ownership verification is a textbook defense against symlink attacks (CWE-59) and race conditions.

[GOOD] Darwin cmdline sourced exclusively from `KERN_PROCARGS2` (kernel-authoritative), with explicit rejection of `ps`-based fallback for ownership decisions. This closes the argv[0] spoofing vector.

[GOOD] DSN hardening (`allowAllFiles=false`, `interpolateParams=false`, explicit timeouts) prevents the MySQL driver from being used as an SSRF or file-read vector against a malicious listener.

---

[ISSUE] TOCTOU gap on Darwin/Windows atomic rename is acknowledged but insufficiently mitigated
  location: internal/doltserver/persist.go (planned)
  category: security
  suggestion: On Darwin, use `renamex_np(RENAME_EXCL)` (available since macOS 10.12) as the equivalent of Linux's `RENAME_NOREPLACE`, falling back to Lstat+Rename only on older kernels. This narrows the window to the same bound as Linux. Document the residual race on Windows as a known limitation bounded by the same-UID trust assumption.
  confidence: medium
  confidence_score: 0.65
  severity_rationale: Exploitable only by a same-UID adversary who can win a tight race on the PID-file path, which the plan already declares as outside the trust boundary — but tightening it is cheap.
  scope: in-diff
  scope_rationale: This is new code being introduced by this change.

[ISSUE] `io.LimitReader` 64KB cap on shellout output sets `Truncated=true` but the plan doesn't specify what happens to the *partial parse* before truncation is detected
  location: internal/doltserver/recover.go (planned IdentityResolver)
  category: security
  suggestion: Ensure `parseDoltSQLServerDataDir` is called ONLY after confirming `Truncated == false`. If the implementation parses argv first and checks truncation second, a crafted process with a 64KB+ cmdline could place `--data-dir=<bd-data-dir>` in the first 64KB and the real `--data-dir=<attacker-dir>` after the cut, causing a false ownership match. The check order must be: read → check truncation → parse. Add a test with a 65KB cmdline where the last `--data-dir` (which wins) is beyond the cap.
  confidence: high
  confidence_score: 0.85
  severity_rationale: If parse-before-truncation-check is implemented, an attacker running as the same UID could craft a process that passes the ownership predicate, leading to PID-file takeover (silent adoption of an adversary-controlled process).
  scope: in-diff
  scope_rationale: This is new parsing logic being introduced.

[SUGGESTION] The plan specifies UID comparison uses real UID but doesn't specify constant-time comparison
  location: internal/doltserver/recover.go (planned checkOwnership)
  category: security
  suggestion: Integer UID comparison is inherently constant-time (`==` on `int`), so this is fine — but document it explicitly in a code comment to prevent a future refactor from switching to string-based UID comparison (e.g., on Windows SID strings) without using `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare`. Windows SID comparison should use `EqualSid()` API, not string equality.
  confidence: medium
  confidence_score: 0.55
  severity_rationale: Timing side-channels on local UID comparison are not practically exploitable, but the Windows SID path could introduce one if not handled carefully.
  scope: in-diff
  scope_rationale: New ownership comparison logic.

[SUGGESTION] The SQL probe connects to an untrusted listener — plan should specify TLS verification posture
  location: internal/doltserver/recover.go (planned SQLProber)
  category: security
  suggestion: Explicitly set `tls=false` or `tls=skip-verify` in the DSN and document that the SQL probe is a liveness check only, not a trust establishment. If the probe were to negotiate TLS with a malicious listener presenting a crafted certificate, and Go's `crypto/tls` had a parsing vulnerability, the probe could be an attack surface. Making TLS opt-out explicit removes ambiguity.
  confidence: medium
  confidence_score: 0.50
  severity_rationale: The probe targets localhost, and TLS negotiation bugs in Go's standard library are rare but not unprecedented; explicit TLS=false eliminates the class entirely.
  scope: in-diff
  scope_rationale: New network connection to potentially untrusted listener.

[SUGGESTION] Windows `Get-CimInstance` output parsing for ProcessIdentity lacks specification of encoding/locale handling
  location: internal/doltserver/recover_windows.go (planned)
  category: security
  suggestion: Pin PowerShell output to UTF-8 via `[Console]::OutputEncoding = [Text.Encoding]::UTF8` or use `-OutputFormat XML` with structured parsing. Locale-dependent output (e.g., localized field names in `wmic`) could cause silent parse failures that bypass identity resolution, degrading to `Owned=false` (safe) but potentially causing persistent recovery failures on non-English Windows systems.
  confidence: medium
  confidence_score: 0.60
  severity_rationale: Fails safe (Owned=false) but could cause the feature to be non-functional on a class of systems, which is a correctness issue more than a security one.
  scope: in-diff
  scope_rationale: New platform-specific code.

---

**Overall assessment**: No blockers. The plan is security-mature — the multi-round council process has addressed the critical issues (process adoption without ownership proof, command injection, symlink attacks, argv spoofing). The two [ISSUE] findings are implementation-order concerns that need explicit attention during coding but don't block the design. Ship it.

findings.suggestion: Integer UID comparison is inherently constant-time (`==` on `int`), so this is fine — but document it explicitly in a code comment to prevent a future refactor from switching to string-based UID comparison (e.g., on Windows SID strings) without using `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare`. Windows SID comparison should use `EqualSid()` API, not string equality.
findings.severity_rationale: Timing side-channels on local UID comparison are not practically exploitable, but the Windows SID path could introduce one if not handled carefully.

findings.finding: The SQL probe connects to an untrusted listener — plan should specify TLS verification posture
findings.suggestion: Explicitly set `tls=false` or `tls=skip-verify` in the DSN and document that the SQL probe is a liveness check only, not a trust establishment. If the probe were to negotiate TLS with a malicious listener presenting a crafted certificate, and Go's `crypto/tls` had a parsing vulnerability, the probe could be an attack surface. Making TLS opt-out explicit removes ambiguity.
findings.severity_rationale: The probe targets localhost, and TLS negotiation bugs in Go's standard library are rare but not unprecedented; explicit TLS=false eliminates the class entirely.
findings.scope_rationale: New network connection to potentially untrusted listener.

findings.finding: Windows `Get-CimInstance` output parsing for ProcessIdentity lacks specification of encoding/locale handling
findings.suggestion: Pin PowerShell output to UTF-8 via `[Console]::OutputEncoding = [Text.Encoding]::UTF8` or use `-OutputFormat XML` with structured parsing. Locale-dependent output (e.g., localized field names in `wmic`) could cause silent parse failures that bypass identity resolution, degrading to `Owned=false` (safe) but potentially causing persistent recovery failures on non-English Windows systems.

action_items.description: Introduce a thin API-mapping layer (`internal reason -> public reason code`) and treat JSON reason codes as a separately versioned contract; keep internal enum free to evolve without forcing backward-compat commitments on implementation details.

action_items.title: The config-resolution architecture is still over-complicated and risks hidden dependency drift between CLI and internal callers
action_items.description: Define one canonical `RecoverParamsProvider` interface in `internal/doltserver` and provide a single implementation in `internal/configadapter`; have both `cmd/bd` and internal paths depend on that interface instead of mixing “cmd helper + internal adapter” narrative. This reduces ambiguity and prevents future shotgun surgery when config precedence changes.

action_items.title: `ResolveAndHealState` is intentionally side-effecting, but using it in `status` still creates command-query tension and cognitive overhead
action_items.description: Keep current behavior, but codify a strict rule: status may heal only PID/port metadata, never process state. Add a dedicated test name and doc invariant for this to prevent future behavior creep.

action_items.title: The plan’s module depth is good, but `Recoverer` is close to becoming a “policy + orchestration + platform coordination” hub
action_items.description: Extract ownership policy into a small `OwnershipEvaluator` (pure) and keep `Recoverer` as orchestration only. This lowers RFC/CBO pressure and keeps extensibility cleaner if new ownership signals are added.

action_items.title: Single-PR delivery is defensible, but review risk is still high for a cross-platform lifecycle change
action_items.description: Keep single PR default, but predefine explicit split trigger criteria (e.g., unresolved review > N days or Windows-specific churn > M comments) and prepared fallback branches to reduce integration risk without changing architectural intent.

action_items.title: Add explicit “non-regression matrix” acceptance bullets for unaffected modes
action_items.description: Add 3-4 explicit checks that embedded mode, non-shared local mode, and existing remote-host external-server status behavior remain unchanged (exit codes + JSON shape). This reduces change-failure risk by making “what must not change” first-class.

action_items.title: Add rollout/abort criteria tied to DORA + SPACE
action_items.description: Define post-merge success thresholds (e.g., median recovery-to-success time, rate of `stop.refused_unowned`, and support incidents for shared-server start/stop). action_items.title: Consider delivery slicing fallback if review stalls

action_items.title: Reduce cognitive load with a short maintainer “operational invariants” appendix
action_items.description: Add a concise invariant list (“never signal unowned PID”, “stdout JSON never polluted”, “persist failure is non-fatal for stop”) and map each to test names. This improves onboarding and long-term maintainability.

action_items.title: Legacy PID revalidation can break healthy running servers if the old bd-spawned process lacks `--data-dir`
action_items.description: Before making legacy `IsRunning` success require the new full ownership predicate, explicitly confirm current released `Start()` always included `--data-dir`. If not, treat legacy PID-file success as trusted legacy state, and apply full ownership only to recovery/stop paths where the PID file is missing or stale.

## Security Review: PID-file Recovery Plan (GH#3687)

This plan is exceptionally well-thought-out from a security perspective. The council iteration process has addressed most concerns I would typically raise. My review focuses on residual risks and areas where implementation could still go wrong.

---

[GOOD] The five-signal ownership predicate (exe path, argv token-exact match, data-dir canonicalization, port binding, UID match) is a strong defense-in-depth design against silent process adoption. This directly addresses CWE-283 (Unverified Ownership).

[GOOD] Argument-array `exec.Command` throughout, with integer-typed PID/port values, eliminates command injection vectors (CWE-78). The plan explicitly bans shell interpolation and tests enforce it.

[GOOD] Atomic PID-file writes with `O_NOFOLLOW`, `O_EXCL`, temp+rename, mode 0600, and parent directory ownership verification is a textbook defense against symlink attacks (CWE-59) and race conditions.

[GOOD] Darwin cmdline sourced exclusively from `KERN_PROCARGS2` (kernel-authoritative), with explicit rejection of `ps`-based fallback for ownership decisions. This closes the argv[0] spoofing vector.

[GOOD] DSN hardening (`allowAllFiles=false`, `interpolateParams=false`, explicit timeouts) prevents the MySQL driver from being used as an SSRF or file-read vector against a malicious listener.

---
